key_insight: Causal effects can be identified and estimated from unpaired data collected across many experimental environments by treating environments as (possibly high-dimensional) instruments and exploiting sparsity in the causal effects.
problem_solved: How to infer causal effects under hidden confounding when covariates X and outcome Y are never observed jointly but come from multiple experimental conditions with few repetitions per condition.
method: Reformulate the unpaired-data problem as an instrumental variable regression where the environment label serves as the instrument.
Leverage many distinct environments (high-dimensional instrument) together with sparsity assumptions on the causal effects to achieve identifiability despite few repeats and hidden confounding.
Provide estimation procedures (regularized/sparse IV methods) and accompanying theoretical guarantees for identification and estimation under regularity conditions.
impact: Enables practitioners to estimate causal effects from fragmented experimental data (many conditions, few samples per condition), expanding causal analysis to settings where X and Y are collected separately and confounding is present.
visual_elements: Schematic showing two datasets side-by-side: one with X across environments, one with Y across environments, emphasizing that X and Y are never paired.
Causal diagram illustrating environment → X → Y with a hidden confounder between X and Y and the environment acting as an instrument.
Bar/needle plot of sparse effect sizes (many zeros, few nonzeros) to convey sparsity assumption and recovered coefficients.
Matrix/heatmap showing many environments (rows) × few repeats, annotated to highlight high-dimensional instrument structure.
paper_title: Many Experiments, Few Repetitions, Unpaired Data, and Sparse Effects: Is Causal Inference Possible?
paper_authors: Felix Schur, Niklas Pfister, Peng Ding, Sach Mukherjee, Jonas Peters
